paragraphs.text: This cake's leaf comes from [Yiwu](greater-yiwu:where-it-is), in the north of Mengla County in Xishuangbanna, on the east side of the Lancang River. It is one of the old Six Famous Tea Mountains, and its town has long been the place where tea from the surrounding villages is gathered and processed.

The leaf was made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition), a method developed to give in weeks what raw pu’er takes years of keeping to become. In [wet piling](shou:wet-piling) the sun-dried leaf is wetted and heaped, and the microbes working in it make their own heat. The pile is covered to hold that heat in and turned about once a week to spread it and let air through. It is kept below about 65°C, because any hotter and the leaf begins to char. After one to two months the leaf is dried, and this lot was then pressed into a cake.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
